lesson.subject: data-ai
lesson.title: True or Fake? Checking What You Find Online
lesson.summary: Learn who makes the web, ask four questions to check a page, spot fakes and scams, and share and credit things responsibly.
learning_objectives: Explain that anyone can publish on the web and every page has a purpose
Check a page with who, why, proof and when, and compare sources
Spot fakes and scams, and share, credit and report responsibly

standards.text: Use technology safely, respectfully and responsibly; be discerning in evaluating digital content
Recognise acceptable and unacceptable behaviour; identify a range of ways to report concerns about content

success_criteria: I can say why we check what we read online
I can ask four questions and compare two sources
I pause before sharing, give credit and tell a trusted adult
lesson.real_life: Deciding whether a forwarded message about free prizes or a surprising news story is true before sharing it with family.

warm_up.explanation: The internet is a network of networks.

options.text: A network that joins computers all over the world

warm_up.prompt: What is a search engine for?

blocks.markdown: Today's big question: how do we tell what is true online?
blocks.say: Today we find out who makes the things we read online. Can we trust all of it?

blocks.alt: Snow-covered mountains and their mirror reflection on a calm blue-green frozen lake
blocks.caption: A reflection looks like the real mountain. Some things online look real but are copies.
blocks.credit: Photo by Tim Stief on Unsplash
blocks.say: This lake shows a mountain and its reflection. A reflection looks real but it is only a copy. Online things can fool us too.

blocks.markdown: The **web** is pages and sites that people publish.
blocks.say: The web is a huge collection of pages that you visit using the internet. People make every page.

blocks.markdown: Anyone with a device can publish on the web.
blocks.say: Schools, shops, news teams and strangers all publish pages. Some are checked by experts. Many are not.

scenes.caption: School.
scenes.say: A school makes a page about its trip to Hunza. Teachers check it.

scenes.caption: Shop.
scenes.say: A shop makes a page to sell trainers. It wants you to buy.

scenes.caption: Stranger.
scenes.say: A stranger makes a page with a shocking claim. Nobody has checked it.

question.prompt: Why should we check what we read on the web?
question.explanation: Many pages are not checked by anyone.

options.text: Because web pages are always long
Because anyone can publish a page, true or not

blocks.text: Stop 2: Every page has a purpose

blocks.markdown: Every page has a **purpose**. Ask why it was made.
blocks.say: A page may teach you, sell something, entertain you, or try to change your mind.

scenes.caption: Inform.
scenes.say: An encyclopedia page wants to inform. It gives facts and names its author.

scenes.caption: Sell.
scenes.say: An advert wants to sell. It shows prices and a buy button.

scenes.caption: Opinion.
scenes.say: A blog post gives an opinion. An opinion is what someone thinks, not always a fact.

question.prompt: A website shows prices and a shopping basket. What is its main purpose?
question.explanation: Prices and baskets mean it wants to sell.

blocks.title: Zara and the free tablets
blocks.transcript: A friend sends Zara a message: free tablets, forward to ten friends! Zara does not forward it. She pauses and thinks. Who made it? There is no author and no website. That is a warning sign. Why was it made? To make her click. There is no proof at all. Zara searches. The tablet company says nothing about a giveaway. She decides it is a scam. It was made to trick people. She tells her teacher, who helps her report the message. The class writes a sharing promise. Pause, check, credit and tell.
blocks.caption: Zara gets a message about free tablets and checks it before sharing.

points: People make the web, and anyone can publish
Every page has a purpose: inform, sell, entertain or persuade
We check pages instead of believing everything
blocks.say: Let us remember. People make the web. Every page has a purpose. We do not believe everything.

blocks.say: Zara asks four questions about a page. Who made it? Why did they make it? What proof is there? When was it written?

scenes.caption: Who.
scenes.say: A page says K2 is about 8,611 metres high. Who made it? A mountain survey, named at the bottom.

blocks.markdown: **Evidence** is proof. Compare **sources** to be sure.
blocks.say: Evidence is proof. When two or more trusted sources agree, a fact is stronger.

scenes.caption: Three sources.
scenes.say: Zara checks a news site, a museum site and her teacher.

scenes.caption: Agree.
scenes.say: All three agree. Now she trusts the fact.

question.explanation: Agreement between trusted sources is a strong sign.

points: Ask who, why, proof and when

blocks.say: Let us remember. Ask four questions and compare sources.

blocks.alt: A clear green lake with snowy mountains and forest, and a faint reflection of the peaks in the water
blocks.caption: Reflections can fool the eye, just as fake posts can fool the mind.
blocks.credit: Photo by Adam Vradenburg on Unsplash
blocks.say: A fake is made to look real so that people believe it. Clear water can show a perfect copy too.

blocks.markdown: A **fake** is made to look real so that people believe it.
blocks.say: Fakes often shout. They use big words, scary news and a push to share quickly.

scenes.caption: Shouting.
scenes.say: A post says: SHOCKING! Share before they delete this! There is no author.

scenes.caption: Too good.
scenes.say: Another says: you won a free tablet! Click now! You never entered a prize draw.

scenes.caption: Likes.
scenes.say: Many likes do not prove anything. Popular is not the same as true.

question.prompt: A post says: SHOCKING news, share in the next ten minutes! It has no author. What does this suggest?
question.explanation: Pressure and no source are warning signs.

options.text: It is from a trusted expert

blocks.markdown: A **scam** tricks you into clicking or giving details.
blocks.say: A scam is a trick to get your details or money. Free prizes you did not enter are a classic sign.

blocks.markdown: Do not click. Tell a grown-up. Play the memory game.
blocks.say: If you are unsure, do not click. Tell a grown-up. First, a memory game.

question.prompt: Which message has a warning sign of a scam? Tap it.
question.hint: Look for a prize and a request for a password.
question.explanation: Nobody should ask for your password to give a prize.

items.label: Prize: send your password to claim
Reminder: the class trip form is due

points: Fakes look real and push you to share
Scams use prizes and ask for details
Likes and views do not prove something is true
blocks.say: Let us remember. Fakes shout, rush and offer prizes. Likes are not proof.

terms.meaning: Made to look real so that people believe it.

blocks.say: Before sharing, Zara pauses. She asks whether it is true, kind and her right to share.

blocks.markdown: Pressure to forward is a warning sign.
blocks.say: She checks the four questions. If a message says forward to ten friends, she is even more careful.
If it is a picture, she asks who made it. She asks permission and gives credit.

scenes.caption: Pause.
scenes.say: A friend sends a message: free tablets, forward to ten friends. Zara pauses.

scenes.caption: Check.
scenes.say: She asks four questions. There is no author, no proof and a rush. It looks fake.

scenes.caption: Do not share.
scenes.say: She does not forward it. She tells her teacher. That keeps friends safe.

question.prompt: Put the steps of handling a suspicious post in order.

items.text: Tell a trusted adult if it worries you
Report it if it is harmful
Stop and do not share it

blocks.markdown: The owner of a picture should get **credit**.
blocks.say: Pictures, music and writing have owners. A fair person asks first and gives credit.

blocks.markdown: **Report** harmful things with a grown-up's help.
blocks.say: If something harmful appears, we tell a trusted adult. We can also use the report button with their help.

scenes.caption: Owned.
scenes.say: Zara wants to use a lovely photo for her poster. The photographer owns it.

scenes.caption: Credit.
scenes.say: She asks permission and writes a credit line. That is fair.

scenes.caption: Report.
scenes.say: A harmful post appears. Zara tells her teacher, who helps her report it.

blocks.title: Our sharing promise

Add one promise about asking permission and giving credit.
Add who you will tell if something worries you.
